warmup.q: Two settlement workers wait on an empty queue with if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); return queue.removeFirst();. The Kafka thread adds one payment and calls notifyAll(). What happens?
options: One worker gets the payment and the other keeps waiting
Both wake; one gets the payment and the other throws NoSuchElementException
notifyAll() wakes only one of them, so nothing goes wrong
warmup.why: notifyAll() wakes both workers, and they take the lock back one at a time. The first one takes the payment. The second one checked its if before it went to sleep, so it calls removeFirst() on an empty queue. With while instead of if, it would check again and go back to waiting. The second section runs exactly this program.

opening:
Picture the settlement queue on a quiet evening. One thread reads card authorizations from Kafka and drops each one into an in-memory queue. A settlement worker takes them off the other end. Between bursts the queue is empty, and the worker waits for the next payment.

So how should it wait? In synchronized and intrinsic locks, we let one thread at a time into the code that touches shared state. That keeps the queue consistent, but a lock says nothing about waiting for the queue to fill. The first versions most of us write either ask the empty queue "anything yet?" millions of times a second, or nap between questions and make each payment wait for the nap to end.

Every Java object has a better answer, built into the monitor that synchronized uses. In this lesson, we'll teach the worker to wait without spinning, see why a second worker must check again, watch notify() stall a bounded queue, and build that queue by hand. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a settlement worker with nothing to do but wait. We gave it a guarded block, a while loop for the second worker and notifyAll() for the bounded queue, and built the buffer that holds them.

Now search your own code for .wait( and .await(. Each should sit in a while loop that tests a state. An if, or a wait with no condition, passes every test until the evening a second worker joins in.

Here, the stalled threads waited with the lock free. Next, we'll meet threads that stop while holding locks: two ledger transfers, each holding one account and waiting for the other. How does that happen, and how do you make sure it can't?

sections.h: Waiting for the queue without spinning: the guarded block
sections.html:
Let's start with one worker and an empty queue. The quickest code asks again and again, taking the lock for every look, since readers need the lock too:

Java
// Naive: asks the empty queue again and again
String nextAuthorization() {
    while (true) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            if (!queue.isEmpty()) return queue.removeFirst();
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
// Naive: asks the empty queue again and again
fun nextAuthorization(): String {
    while (true) {
        synchronized(lock) {
            if (queue.isNotEmpty()) return queue.removeFirst()
        }
    }
}

That loop is correct: it never takes a payment that isn't there, and it never misses one. But it's a busy wait, or spin. The thread stays RUNNABLE and keeps a core busy the whole time it waits, and the Kafka thread has to compete with it for the lock on every add.

The Try it below times a simpler spinner, one that checks a volatile flag, against a thread that waits properly. To wait one second, the spinner used about 1,030 ms of CPU. The waiting thread used 0 ms.

A Thread.sleep(50) between looks saves the CPU. In exchange, a payment that lands just after a look sits there for up to 50 ms. The outbox relay in A thread's life made the same trade between its polls. A sleep is a guess about when the next item will arrive, and the guess is never quite right.

What we want is a worker that sleeps until the queue changes, and a Kafka thread that wakes it when it does. Every Java object can do that, through its monitor. Here's the worker's side:

Java
// Fixed: sleeps until a payment arrives
String nextAuthorization() throws InterruptedException {
    synchronized (lock) {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) {
            lock.wait();               // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take it again
        }
        return queue.removeFirst();    // the queue has an item, and we hold the lock
    }
}
Kotlin
// Fixed: sleeps until a payment arrives
fun nextAuthorization(): String {
    synchronized(lock) {               // lock is a java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait()
        while (queue.isEmpty()) {
            lock.wait()                // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take it again
        }
        return queue.removeFirst()     // the queue has an item, and we hold the lock
    }
}

wait() does three things, in order. First, it releases the monitor, so the Kafka thread can get in. Then it parks the worker in the monitor's wait set, in the WAITING state, using no CPU. Finally, when the worker is woken, it takes the monitor back before wait() returns. So the line after wait() runs with the lock held, like the line before it.

The Kafka thread does the other half, holding the same lock:

Java
void add(String authorization) {
    synchronized (lock) {
        queue.addLast(authorization);  // change the state first
        lock.notifyAll();              // then wake every thread waiting on lock
    }
}
Kotlin
fun add(authorization: String) {
    synchronized(lock) {
        queue.addLast(authorization)   // change the state first
        lock.notifyAll()               // then wake every thread waiting on lock
    }
}

notifyAll() doesn't hand over the lock. Each woken thread moves to the monitor's entry set, the threads queuing to get in, and shows as BLOCKED until the Kafka thread leaves its block. (Its sibling notify() wakes just one waiter. Which one it wakes will matter in the third section.)

Picture the monitor as a room with one key. wait() hangs the key on its hook and steps into the waiting room next door. notifyAll() sends everyone in the waiting room back to the corridor, to queue for the key again. The waiting room is the wait set, and the corridor is the entry set; the figure draws both.

The worker's code is a guarded block. The guard is the loop's condition, here "the queue isn't empty", and the thread waits until it holds. Notice that the guard is a while, although with one worker an if looks just as good. We'll come back to that in the next section.

The order on the Kafka side matters too: state first, then the signal. If a payment arrives before the worker starts waiting, the notifyAll() wakes nobody, and that's fine. The worker checks the queue first, finds the payment and never calls wait(). Code that waits for a bare signal, with no state to check, sleeps forever when the signal comes first. That's a lost wake-up, and it passes tests because the waiter usually gets there first.

A notification is only a hint. Wait for a state, never for a signal.

One more rule holds it all together. You must hold the monitor of the object you call wait() or notifyAll() on, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException at once. Since the queue can change only under the lock, no payment can slip in between the worker's check and its wait.

One worker now waits for free and wakes the moment a payment lands. A busy evening needs a second one.

try.title: Spin vs wait
steps: Read BusyWaitDemo. Both threads wait one second for the same event: the spinner checks a volatile flag, and the waiter sits in a guarded block. Write down your guess for each thread's CPU time.
In the waiter, delete the synchronized line around the while loop and its closing brace, so lock.wait() runs without the lock. Predict what happens, run it, then put the lines back.

code.title: BusyWaitDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two threads wait one second for the same flag. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. */ public class BusyWaitDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); static boolean ready; // guarded by lock static volatile boolean readyForSpinner; // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs volatile public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinner = new Thread(() -> { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can }, "spinner"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait(); // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } } } }, "waiter"); spinner.start(); waiter.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // the authorization takes a second to come back ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinner.threadId()) / 1_000_000; // measure while both still wait long waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waiter.threadId()) / 1_000_000; readyForSpinner = true; synchronized (lock) { ready = true; lock.notifyAll(); // wake the waiter; it runs once we leave this block } spinner.join(); waiter.join(); System.out.printf("spinner used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", spinCpu); System.out.printf("waiter used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", waitCpu); } }

alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two threads wait one second for the same flag. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() private var ready = false // guarded by lock @Volatile private var readyForSpinner = false // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs @Volatile fun main() { val spinner = thread(name = "spinner") { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can } val waiter = thread(name = "waiter") { synchronized(lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait() // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() return@thread } } } } Thread.sleep(1_000) // the authorization takes a second to come back val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinner.threadId()) / 1_000_000 // measure while both still wait val waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waiter.threadId()) / 1_000_000 readyForSpinner = true synchronized(lock) { ready = true lock.notifyAll() // wake the waiter; it runs once we leave this block } spinner.join() waiter.join() println("spinner used about $spinCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") println("waiter used about $waitCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") }

try.expect: The spinner uses about a full second of CPU to wait one second (runs here printed 1,022 to 1,037 ms). The waiter uses 0 ms. Without the synchronized block, the waiter dies at once with IllegalMonitorStateException: you can only wait on a monitor you hold.

aside.title: Why do the Kotlin samples lock on Object()?
aside.html: Kotlin's Any stands for java.lang.Object, but it doesn't expose wait(), notify() or notifyAll(). To call them, the Kotlin samples in this lesson declare the lock as a java.lang.Object itself, private val lock = Object(), which earns a compiler warning that the demos silence with @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN"). The idiomatic Kotlin guarded block uses a ReentrantLock and a Condition instead: await() plays the part of wait(), and signalAll() the part of notifyAll(). Every rule in this lesson holds there unchanged, and lesson 7 of this track covers it.

sections.h: A second worker, and why every wait sits in a while loop
sections.html:
Remember the while in the worker's guard? With one worker, an if seems to do the same job: check once, wait if the queue is empty, then take the payment. Plenty of first versions look exactly like this:

Java
// Naive: checks once, before waiting
synchronized (lock) {
    if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait();
    return queue.removeFirst();
}
Kotlin
// Naive: checks once, before waiting
synchronized(lock) {
    if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait()
    return queue.removeFirst()
}

With one worker, that passes every test. So let's give it a second worker and a single payment. The Try it below parks two consumers in wait(), adds one authorization and calls notifyAll(). Here's what it printed:

consumer-2 failed: java.util.NoSuchElementException
consumer-1 took auth-1

notifyAll() woke two workers for one payment, and the second one found the queue empty. Let's trace it, one thread at a time:

  1. Both workers find the queue empty and call wait(), so both sit in the wait set.
  2. The Kafka thread adds auth-1 and calls notifyAll(). Both workers move to the entry set.
  3. Consumer 1 gets the lock first. Its wait() returns, it takes auth-1, and it leaves.
  4. Consumer 2 gets the lock next, and its wait() returns too. Its if ran long ago, before it waited, so it goes straight to removeFirst() on an empty queue.

Which worker wins, and which line prints first, changes from run to run. The ending doesn't.

With while, consumer 2 checks the queue again after waking, finds it empty and goes back to waiting. Change that one word in the Try it, and the second worker waits quietly until main gives it auth-2.

Being woken doesn't mean the state is right. Check again, in a while loop.

There's a second reason for the loop, in the Javadoc for Object.wait: "A thread can wake up without being notified, interrupted, or timing out, a so-called spurious wakeup." It's rare, but it's allowed, and the Javadoc tells you to test the condition again and keep waiting. In the waiting-room picture, nobody walks out for no reason; a Java thread is allowed to. So even a lone worker needs the loop. A second worker just makes the bug show up on the first busy evening.

The loop costs nothing, so use it every time. In a code review, treat an if around wait() as a bug, even in code that has never failed. It just hasn't had two waiters at once yet.

Two workers now share the queue safely. But nothing stops the Kafka thread from adding payments faster than the workers can settle them. Next, we'll give the queue a limit, and the waiting starts on the other side too.

try.title: Steal a wake-up
steps: Read IfInsteadOfWhile. Both consumers are parked in wait() before main adds one item and calls notifyAll().
Run it and read both consumers' lines.
Change if (queue.isEmpty()) to while (queue.isEmpty()). Write down what you expect each consumer to print, then run it again.

code.title: IfInsteadOfWhile.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Two consumers wait on an empty queue. One item arrives. The guard is an `if`. */ public class IfInsteadOfWhile { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); static String take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait(); } return queue.removeFirst(); // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Runnable consumer = () -> { try { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " took " + take()); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " failed: " + e); } }; Thread c1 = new Thread(consumer, "consumer-1"); Thread c2 = new Thread(consumer, "consumer-2"); c1.start(); c2.start(); while (c1.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10); // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized (lock) { queue.addLast("auth-1"); // one item... lock.notifyAll(); // ...and both consumers wake up } c1.join(2_000); c2.join(2_000); if (c1.isAlive() || c2.isAlive()) { // with `while`, one consumer goes back to waiting System.out.println("one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item"); synchronized (lock) { queue.addLast("auth-2"); lock.notifyAll(); } } c1.join(); c2.join(); } }

alt.title: IfInsteadOfWhile.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque // Two consumers wait on an empty queue. One item arrives. The guard is an `if`. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val queue = ArrayDeque<String>() private fun take(): String { synchronized(lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait() } return queue.removeFirst() // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } fun main() { val consumer = Runnable { try { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} took ${take()}") } catch (e: Exception) { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} failed: $e") } } val c1 = Thread(consumer, "consumer-1") val c2 = Thread(consumer, "consumer-2") c1.start() c2.start() while (c1.state != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.state != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10) // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized(lock) { queue.addLast("auth-1") // one item... lock.notifyAll() // ...and both consumers wake up } c1.join(2_000) c2.join(2_000) if (c1.isAlive || c2.isAlive) { // with `while`, one consumer goes back to waiting println("one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item") synchronized(lock) { queue.addLast("auth-2") lock.notifyAll() } } c1.join() c2.join() }

try.expect: With if: one consumer takes auth-1 and the other fails with java.util.NoSuchElementException. With while: one consumer takes auth-1, the other checks again and goes back to waiting, main prints one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item, and that consumer takes auth-2. Which consumer wins can change from run to run.

video.title: Two consumers, one payment: notifyAll wakes both, so a woken thread must check again in a while loop

sections.h: A limit on the queue, and why notify() can stall it
sections.html:
So far only the workers wait. When the card network slows down, the workers fall behind, the Kafka thread keeps adding, and an unbounded queue grows until the heap runs out. So let's give the queue a capacity, and make the Kafka thread wait while it's full:

Java
while (queue.size() == capacity) lock.wait();   // the Kafka thread's guard: "not full"
Kotlin
while (queue.size == capacity) lock.wait()      // the Kafka thread's guard: "not full"

Making a fast producer wait for a slow consumer like this is called backpressure. It also gives the monitor two kinds of waiters. The Kafka thread waits for "not full", and the workers wait for "not empty". A monitor has only one wait set, so they all wait in the same place.

With notifyAll(), that's harmless: everyone wakes, and each while loop sends back the threads that can't go on. With notify(), it isn't. notify() wakes one waiter, and it doesn't take requests: the JVM picks which one. Here's what that does to a one-slot queue with two producers and two consumers, where every signal is a notify():

  1. The slot is empty, so both consumers wait.
  2. Producer 1 fills the slot, and its notify() wakes consumer 1. Before consumer 1 gets the lock, both producers find the slot full and wait. The wait set now holds producer 1, producer 2 and consumer 2.
  3. Consumer 1 empties the slot and calls notify(), which happens to wake consumer 2, the wrong kind.
  4. Consumer 2 finds the slot empty and waits again. Consumer 1 loops back, finds it empty too, and waits.

Now all four threads wait for a signal nobody is left to send. No thread holds the lock, so this isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense (the next lesson has those), but the pipeline has stopped just the same. The Try it below gets there fast. One run printed:

using notify()
after 1 s: 5 items moved
stalled after 5 items. Thread states:
  producer-0: WAITING
  producer-1: WAITING
  consumer-0: WAITING
  consumer-1: WAITING

Across runs here it stalled after 1 to 5 items. With both signals switched to notifyAll(), the same four threads moved about 139,000 items in five seconds and never stalled. Each thread of the wrong kind checks its guard and goes back to waiting, so the right kind always gets a turn. The price is some extra wake-ups, which is cheap next to a stalled pipeline.

Two kinds of waiters on one monitor need notifyAll(). Wake them all, and let each loop decide.

notify() is safe only when every waiter waits for the same condition and one change lets at most one of them go on. Our unbounded queue from the first two sections qualified: only workers waited, and one payment let one worker go. A bounded queue never does. For a precise wake-up per kind of waiter, give each kind its own Condition on a ReentrantLock, as lesson 7 of this track shows.

We now have all three pieces: a loop around every wait(), a change of state before every signal, and notifyAll() when the waiters differ. Let's put them together.

try.title: Stall a pipeline with notify()
steps: Run NotifyStall. Two producers and two consumers share a one-slot buffer, and every signal is a notify().
When progress stops, read the thread states it prints and match them against the four steps in this section.
Predict whether it stalls with notifyAll(). Then run it again with -Pargs=all, which switches both signals to notifyAll().

code.title: NotifyStall.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A one-slot buffer shared by 2 producers and 2 consumers. Uses notify(), or notifyAll() with -Pargs=all. */ public class NotifyStall { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<Integer> slot = new ArrayDeque<>(); static final AtomicLong moved = new AtomicLong(); static boolean all; // set once in main, before the threads start static void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (!slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); slot.addLast(x); signal(); // notify() wakes ONE waiter: maybe a consumer, maybe the other producer } } static int take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); int x = slot.removeFirst(); signal(); return x; } } static void signal() { if (all) lock.notifyAll(); else lock.notify(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { all = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("all"); System.out.println(all ? "using notifyAll()" : "using notify()"); Thread[] threads = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { boolean producer = i < 2; threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (true) { if (producer) put(1); else { take(); moved.incrementAndGet(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, (producer ? "producer-" : "consumer-") + (i % 2)); threads[i].setDaemon(true); threads[i].start(); } long last = -1; for (int second = 1; second <= 5; second++) { Thread.sleep(1_000); long now = moved.get(); if (now == last) { System.out.printf("stalled after %,d items. Thread states:%n", now); for (Thread t : threads) System.out.println(" " + t.getName() + ": " + t.getState()); return; } System.out.printf("after %d s: %,d items moved%n", second, now); last = now; } System.out.println(all ? "no stall: notifyAll() wakes every waiter, so the right kind always gets a turn" : "no stall this time; it depends on timing, so run it again"); } }

alt.title: NotifyStall.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong // A one-slot buffer shared by 2 producers and 2 consumers. Uses notify(), or notifyAll() with -Pargs=all. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val slot = ArrayDeque<Int>() private val moved = AtomicLong() private var all = false // set once in main, before the threads start private fun put(x: Int) { synchronized(lock) { while (!slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait() slot.addLast(x) signal() // notify() wakes ONE waiter: maybe a consumer, maybe the other producer } } private fun take(): Int { synchronized(lock) { while (slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait() val x = slot.removeFirst() signal() return x } } private fun signal() { if (all) lock.notifyAll() else lock.notify() } fun main(args: Array<String>) { all = args.firstOrNull() == "all" println(if (all) "using notifyAll()" else "using notify()") val threads = List(4) { i -> val producer = i < 2 Thread({ try { while (true) { if (producer) put(1) else { take(); moved.incrementAndGet() } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } }, (if (producer) "producer-" else "consumer-") + (i % 2)).apply { isDaemon = true start() } } var last = -1L for (second in 1..5) { Thread.sleep(1_000) val now = moved.get() if (now == last) { println("stalled after %,d items. Thread states:".format(now)) threads.forEach { println(" ${it.name}: ${it.state}") } return } println("after %d s: %,d items moved".format(second, now)) last = now } println(if (all) "no stall: notifyAll() wakes every waiter, so the right kind always gets a turn" else "no stall this time; it depends on timing, so run it again") }

try.expect: With notify() it stalls almost at once (after 1 to 5 items in runs here), with all four threads WAITING. With notifyAll() it never stalls, and moves roughly 28,000 items a second for the full five seconds. Your counts will differ. On a rare run notify() survives the five seconds; run it again, and it almost always stalls.

sections.h: The bounded buffer, built by hand, and where it stops
sections.html:
Put the three pieces together and you get the class you'll write in the lab: a bounded buffer, which is the settlement queue with a capacity. The Kafka thread waits in put() when the workers fall behind, and the workers wait in take() when there's nothing to settle:

Java
public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;

    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (items.size() == capacity) {   // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up
                lock.wait();
            }
            items.addLast(item);                 // 2. act: condition holds, lock held
            lock.notifyAll();                    // 3. signal: the state changed
        }
    }

    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (items.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait();
            }
            T head = items.removeFirst();
            lock.notifyAll();
            return head;
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) {
    @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN")
    private val lock = Object()                    // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait()
    private val items = ArrayDeque<T>()

    @Throws(InterruptedException::class)           // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version
    fun put(item: T) {
        synchronized(lock) {
            while (items.size == capacity) {       // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up
                lock.wait()
            }
            items.addLast(item)                    // 2. act: condition holds, lock held
            lock.notifyAll()                       // 3. signal: the state changed
        }
    }

    @Throws(InterruptedException::class)
    fun take(): T {
        synchronized(lock) {
            while (items.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait()
            }
            val head = items.removeFirst()
            lock.notifyAll()
            return head
        }
    }
}

put() and take() have the same three parts. The guard is the while loop that waits until the method can go on. The act changes the queue, safely, because the condition holds and the lock is held. The signal wakes the other side, because the state it waits on just changed. Read put() aloud and it says: while there's no room, wait; add the item; tell everyone something changed.

Three smaller choices are deliberate, and each comes from an earlier lesson. The lock is a private object, as synchronized and intrinsic locks recommended, so only the buffer can wait on it or signal it. Both methods signal with notifyAll(), because producers and consumers share one wait set. And both declare throws InterruptedException. The buffer can't know what its caller wants to do about an interrupt, so it lets the exception propagate, one of the two good answers from A thread's life.

Now the honest part. In production you won't write this class: ArrayBlockingQueue does the same job, with timeouts, and lesson 9 of this track covers it. Our buffer also has a cost built in. With one wait set, every notifyAll() wakes producers and consumers alike, and most of them check their guard and go straight back to waiting. A Condition gives one lock a separate wait set per condition, and lesson 7 of this track builds on that.

Why build it, then? Because you meet guarded blocks every day, inside libraries. A connection pool with 20 connections makes the 21st request wait. A KafkaProducer blocks send() for up to max.block.ms when its buffer is full. In a thread dump, those threads show WAITING or TIMED_WAITING inside the library's code. Once you've written put() and take() yourself, the stack tells you which condition they wait for.

Check your model before you start the lab. Delete the notifyAll() in take(). Two producers fill a buffer of capacity 2 and then wait in put(). A consumer takes one item. What happens next? (The producers stay in wait(): the take made room, but nothing woke them. The consumers drain the buffer and then wait too, until every thread is waiting.)

compare.title: A guarded buffer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BoundedBuffer.java
java.html: public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } }

kotlin.title: KotlinGuarded.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Kotlin's Any has no wait()/notify(). The idiomatic guarded block uses a Lock and a Condition. class KotlinBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() // one wait set, like a monitor's private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) changed.await() // same while-loop guard items.addLast(item) changed.signalAll() // same as notifyAll() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) changed.await() items.removeFirst().also { changed.signalAll() } } } fun main() { val buffer = KotlinBuffer<Int>(2) val consumer = thread { repeat(5) { println("took ${buffer.take()}") } } repeat(5) { buffer.put(it) } consumer.join() }

compare.note: Both versions are the same guarded buffer: the same while guard, the same act, and the same signal to every waiter. Three things changed in the Kotlin one. lock.withLock { } takes and releases a ReentrantLock where Java writes synchronized. changed.await() stands in for wait(). And changed.signalAll() stands in for notifyAll(). The Java version uses the monitor that every object has carried since Java 1.0, and it needs nothing else. The Kotlin version reaches for a Condition because Kotlin's Any doesn't expose wait(). The rules don't change with the tool: Condition allows spurious wakeups too, so the while stays. What the Condition adds is room to grow, because one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers could wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds exactly that.

worked.title: Wait for a settlement file, with a deadline

steps.say: A batch job must wait until the card network's settlement file has arrived, and give up after 30 seconds. Here is the first attempt. Before you read on, find what can go wrong.
steps.code: boolean awaitFile() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (!fileArrived) lock.wait(30_000); return fileArrived; } }

alt.html: fun awaitFile(): Boolean { synchronized(lock) { if (!fileArrived) lock.wait(30_000) return fileArrived } }

steps.say: It's the if bug in a new shape. A spurious wakeup, or a notifyAll() meant for some other condition on the same lock, makes wait() return early with fileArrived still false: after 2 seconds, say, instead of 30. Just moving wait(30_000) into a while loop is wrong too, because every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The cure is to set the deadline once and wait only for what's left of it.
The guard loop now checks two things: the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the time that's left.
steps.code: boolean awaitFile(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos(); // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized (lock) { while (!fileArrived) { // 2. guard on the condition long leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000; if (leftMillis <= 0) return false; // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis); // 4. wait only for what's left } return true; } }

alt.html: fun awaitFile(timeout: Duration): Boolean { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos() // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized(lock) { while (!fileArrived) { // 2. guard on the condition val leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000 if (leftMillis <= 0) return false // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis) // 4. wait only for what's left } return true } }

steps.say: The thread that receives the file sets the state before it signals, both under the lock, just as the Kafka thread did. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter sees fileArrived and never calls wait(). One question before the last step: why does the waiter use System.nanoTime() and not System.currentTimeMillis()?
steps.code: void onFileArrived() { synchronized (lock) { fileArrived = true; // state first lock.notifyAll(); // then the signal } }

alt.html: fun onFileArrived() { synchronized(lock) { fileArrived = true // state first lock.notifyAll() // then the signal } }

steps.say: nanoTime() only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. currentTimeMillis() is wall-clock time, and NTP can move it backwards or forwards, which would stretch or cut the timeout.

lab.title: Build a bounded buffer with wait and notifyAll
steps: Run the tests. All six fail, some only after a few seconds, because the threads that should wait die instead.
Add the fields: a private lock object, an ArrayDeque for the items, the capacity. Reject a capacity below 1 in the constructor.
Write put: guard with while (full) lock.wait();, add at the tail, then notifyAll().
Write take: guard with while (empty) lock.wait();, remove the head, notifyAll(), and return it. Write size() under the lock.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more. The test with four producers and four consumers is the one that catches if and notify() mistakes.
hints: The blocking tests poll getState() until it says WAITING. A thread that sleeps in a loop shows TIMED_WAITING and fails them. Use wait() with no timeout.
Call wait() and notifyAll() on the same object you synchronize on. Calling wait() on this while holding lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException.
Don't catch InterruptedException inside the buffer. Let it propagate: both methods already declare it.
lab.done: All six tests in BoundedBufferTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A bounded buffer from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. In a blank file, write a bounded buffer of String with put and take, using synchronized, wait and notifyAll. Then check your work: is every wait() inside a while? Do both methods signal? Did you lock on a private object?

answer.html: public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() @Throws(InterruptedException::class) // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version fun put(item: T) { synchronized(lock) { while (items.size == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait() } items.addLast(item) // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll() // 3. signal: the state changed } } @Throws(InterruptedException::class) fun take(): T { synchronized(lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait() } val head = items.removeFirst() lock.notifyAll() return head } } }

recap: A guarded block holds the lock, checks a condition, and calls wait() until the condition holds. wait() gives the monitor back while it waits and takes it again before it returns.
Call wait(), notify() or notifyAll() only while holding that object's monitor, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException.
Always while (!condition) wait();. Another woken thread may change the state before you get the lock back, and spurious wakeups are allowed.
Change the state, then notify. Wait for a state, never for a bare signal, so an early notification is never lost.
notify() wakes one waiter of the JVM's choosing. With two kinds of waiters on one monitor it can wake the wrong kind and stall everything, so default to notifyAll().
The limit: a monitor has one wait set, so every notifyAll() wakes every kind of waiter. A Condition gives each kind its own (lesson 7), and ArrayBlockingQueue does the whole job for you (lesson 9).

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a bounded buffer built on one monitor needs while loops and notifyAll(), and what goes wrong if you use if or notify() instead.
explain.answer: Producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty", but with one monitor they share one wait set. When a thread wakes, the state may already have changed again, because other woken threads can get the lock first, and spurious wakeups are allowed. So each waiter must check its condition again in a while loop. With if, a consumer can wake up and remove from an empty buffer. notify() wakes one waiter of the JVM's choosing, which may be the wrong kind: a consumer waking another consumer wastes the only signal, and soon every thread waits with nobody left to wake them. notifyAll() wakes everyone, and the loops send the ones that can't go on back to waiting.

deeper.html:
Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. wait(millis) returns when it's notified, interrupted, woken spuriously, or when the time is up, and it doesn't tell you which. That's why the worked example tracks its own deadline with System.nanoTime().

The JVM has had bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That's one more reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write.

Two notes on observing waits. JFR has a jdk.JavaMonitorWait event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a jdk.JavaMonitorNotify event. And on virtual threads, Object.wait() used to pin the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases.

Finally, the history. wait and notify have been in Java since 1.0. java.util.concurrent arrived in Java 5 with Condition, BlockingQueue and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. Read the source of ArrayBlockingQueue and you'll find the same guard, act and signal as in this lesson, written with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions.
